name: Appeal to probability
description: Taking something for granted because it would probably be the case (or might possibly be the case).

name: Argument from fallacy
description: Assuming that if a particular argument for a conclusion is fallacious, the conclusion itself must be false.

name: Base rate fallacy
description: Making a probability judgement based on conditional probabilities without accounting for prior (base rate) probabilities.

name: Conjunction fallacy
description: Assuming an outcome satisfying multiple conditions is more probable than an outcome satisfying just one of them.

name: Masked-man fallacy
description: Substituting identical designators in a true statement in a way that leads to a false one.

name: Affirming a disjunct
description: Concluding that one part of 'A or B' must be false because the other part, A, is true.

name: Affirming the consequent
description: Claiming the antecedent of a conditional is true merely because the consequent is true (if A then B; B, therefore A).

name: Denying the antecedent
description: Claiming the consequent of a conditional is false merely because the antecedent is false (if A then B; not A, therefore not B).

name: Existential fallacy
description: An argument with a universal premise that jumps to a particular conclusion.

name: Fallacy of the undistributed middle
description: A categorical syllogism where the middle term is never actually distributed, so it can't connect the other two terms.

name: Modal fallacy
description: Confusing something that is merely necessary for an outcome with something that is sufficient to cause it.

name: Modal scope fallacy
description: Placing an unwarranted degree of necessity into the conclusion of an argument.

name: Argument from incredulity
description: Deeming something false because you can't imagine it being true (or true because you can't imagine it being false).

name: Argument to moderation
description: Assuming the middle-ground compromise between two positions must be correct.

name: Continuum fallacy
description: Improperly rejecting a claim just because it's imprecise or lacks a sharp boundary.

name: Suppressed correlative
description: Redefining a term so that one alternative to it becomes impossible (e.g. 'I'm not fat, I'm just thinner than John').

name: Divine fallacy
description: Arguing that something so amazing or improbable must be the work of a divine, alien, or paranormal cause.

name: Doorman fallacy
description: Judging a role only by its most visible task, ignoring the value that isn't obvious on paper.

name: Double counting
description: Counting the same event or piece of evidence more than once in a probability or evidence argument.

name: Ecological fallacy
description: Inferring something about an individual purely from statistics about the group they belong to.

name: Equivocation
description: Using a word with more than one meaning in the same argument without clarifying which meaning is meant.

name: Definitional retreat
description: Quietly changing the meaning of a key word once your original claim is challenged.

name: Motte-and-bailey fallacy
description: Defending an easy, modest claim (the motte) while actually trying to win support for a bolder, more controversial one (the bailey).

name: Fallacy of accent
description: Changing a statement's meaning by leaving its emphasis or stress ambiguous.

name: Persuasive definition
description: Passing off a biased, altered definition of a word as if it were the plain, commonly accepted one.

name: Etymological fallacy
description: Assuming a word's original or historical meaning must still govern its present-day use.

name: Fallacy of composition
description: Assuming something true of a part must also be true of the whole it belongs to.

name: Fallacy of division
description: Assuming something true of a whole must also be true of each of its parts.

name: False attribution
description: Backing an argument with an irrelevant, unqualified, unidentified, or fabricated source.

name: Fallacy of quoting out of context
description: Selectively excerpting words from their original context to twist their intended meaning.

name: False authority
description: Leaning on an expert of dubious credentials, or just one lone opinion, to settle a claim.

name: False dilemma
description: Presenting only two options as if they were the only ones possible, when more actually exist.

name: False equivalence
description: Describing two things as basically equal when they're really not comparable.

name: Historian's fallacy
description: Assuming people in the past had the same information available that we have now when judging their decisions.

name: If-by-whiskey
description: Arguing 'for' an issue using terms so emotionally loaded and vague that they secretly support both sides.

name: Incomplete comparison
description: Making a comparison ('better', 'safer', 'more') without giving enough information to actually evaluate it.

name: Kettle logic
description: Defending a position with several excuses that are mutually inconsistent with each other.

name: McNamara fallacy
description: Arguing from numbers and measurements alone while discounting qualities that can't be quantified.

name: Moving the goalposts
description: Dismissing evidence that meets your original demand and requiring even more (or different) evidence instead.

name: Nirvana fallacy
description: Rejecting a workable solution because it isn't a perfect one.

name: Package deal
description: Treating two essentially different ideas as if they must stand or fall together.

name: Proof by assertion
description: Just repeating a claim over and over, regardless of any counter-evidence, as if repetition made it true.

name: Proving too much
description: Using logic that, if actually valid, would also prove an absurd conclusion nobody accepts.

name: Reification
description: Treating an abstract idea or hypothetical construct as if it were a concrete, physical, real thing.

name: Slippery slope
description: Claiming a small first step will inevitably trigger a chain reaction ending in some extreme, terrible outcome.

name: Special pleading
description: Claiming your case is a special exception to a rule, without giving any real justification for the exemption.

name: Begging the question
description: Sneaking the conclusion you're trying to prove into one of your own premises.

name: Circular reasoning
description: Supporting a claim with a reason that ultimately just restates the claim itself.

name: Loaded label
description: Using an emotionally loaded term (e.g. 'safe', 'natural') so its connotation does the arguing for you.

name: Fallacy of many questions
description: Asking a loaded question that already presupposes something unproven (e.g. 'Have you stopped cheating yet?').

name: Accident
description: Applying a general rule to a specific case where an obvious exception should apply.

name: No true Scotsman
description: Saving a generalization from a counterexample by redefining the group to conveniently exclude it.

name: Cherry picking
description: Presenting only the examples or data that support your position while ignoring the ones that don't.

name: Nut-picking
description: Hunting out the most fringe, unrepresentative voice in an opposing group and treating it as representative of the whole.

name: Survivorship bias
description: Judging by the successes you can see while ignoring all the invisible failures.

name: False analogy
description: Comparing two things that aren't actually similar enough for the comparison to hold.

name: Hasty generalization
description: Drawing a broad conclusion from a sample that's too small or unrepresentative.

name: Argument from anecdote
description: Treating a single personal story as if it were solid evidence for a general claim.

name: Misleading vividness
description: Describing a rare, dramatic case so vividly that it seems far more common or important than it is.

name: Overwhelming exception
description: Qualifying a generalization with so many exceptions that almost nothing is left of the original claim.

name: Thought-terminating cliché
description: Ending an argument with a canned phrase that sounds wise but actually dodges the point.

name: Cum hoc ergo propter hoc
description: Assuming that because two things are correlated, one must have caused the other.

name: Post hoc ergo propter hoc
description: Assuming X caused Y simply because X happened before Y.

name: Wrong direction
description: Getting cause and effect backwards, treating the actual effect as if it were the cause.

name: Fallacy of the single cause
description: Pinning an outcome on one simple cause when it really had several contributing causes.

name: Furtive fallacy
description: Assuming an outcome must be the result of someone's hidden wrongdoing.

name: Magical thinking
description: Believing that a thought, ritual, or unrelated action directly caused a real-world outcome.

name: Regression fallacy
description: Assigning a cause to what is really just a natural statistical fluctuation back toward the average.

name: Gambler's fallacy
description: Believing that independent random events (like coin flips) are 'due' to balance out.

name: Inverse gambler's fallacy
description: Assuming an unlikely outcome proves the underlying process must have run many times before.

name: Sunk cost fallacy
description: Sticking with a losing course of action just because of the time or effort already put into it.

name: Appeal to the stone
description: Dismissing a claim as absurd without ever actually demonstrating why it's absurd.

name: Invincible ignorance
description: Simply refusing to believe an argument no matter what evidence is given.

name: Argument from ignorance
description: Claiming something is true because it hasn't been proven false (or false because it hasn't been proven true).

name: Argument from repetition
description: Repeating a claim until people stop objecting, then treating the silence as proof it's true.

name: Argument from silence
description: Assuming a claim is true because a source that should mention it doesn't.

name: Ignoratio elenchi
description: Making a technically valid argument that simply doesn't address the actual question at hand.

name: Red herring
description: Introducing an irrelevant point to drag attention away from the actual topic.

name: Ad hominem
description: Attacking the person making the argument instead of addressing the argument itself.

name: Circumstantial ad hominem
description: Dismissing someone's conclusion just because they personally benefit from it.

name: Poisoning the well
description: Preemptively trashing someone's credibility so anything they say afterward gets dismissed.

name: Appeal to motive
description: Dismissing an idea by questioning why the person is bringing it up, instead of addressing the idea.

name: Tone policing
description: Criticizing how emotionally someone said something instead of engaging with what they said.

name: Bulverism
description: Assuming an argument is wrong because of the psychological motives behind it, without refuting it.

name: Appeal to authority
description: Treating a claim as true mainly because an authority figure said it, regardless of the actual evidence.

name: Appeal to accomplishment
description: Judging a claim true or false based on the achievements (or lack thereof) of the person making it.

name: Courtier's reply
description: Dismissing a critic by claiming they lack the credentials to comment, instead of answering the criticism.

name: Appeal to consequences
description: Arguing a claim is true or false based on whether believing it leads to good or bad outcomes.

name: Appeal to emotion
description: Trying to win agreement by stirring up feelings instead of offering sound reasoning.

name: Appeal to fear
description: Trying to win an argument by making the audience anxious or afraid.

name: Appeal to flattery
description: Buttering someone up with insincere praise to win their agreement.

name: Appeal to pity
description: Trying to win agreement by making the audience feel sorry for you.

name: Appeal to ridicule
description: Mocking the opposing position instead of engaging with its actual merits.

name: Appeal to spite
description: Stirring up bitterness or hostility toward an opponent to win the argument.

name: Judgmental language
description: Loading your argument with insults or pejorative wording instead of substance.

name: Pooh-pooh
description: Waving off an opposing argument as beneath consideration, without engaging it.

name: Style over substance
description: Dressing up an argument in slick or catchy language to make weak reasoning feel persuasive.

name: Wishful thinking
description: Arguing for what you'd like to be true rather than what the evidence supports.

name: Appeal to nature
description: Judging something as good or bad purely based on whether it's 'natural'.

name: Appeal to novelty
description: Claiming something is better purely because it's new or modern.

name: Appeal to poverty
description: Supporting a conclusion because its proponent is poor (or dismissing it because they're wealthy).

name: Appeal to tradition
description: Defending a claim solely because it's the way things have always been done.

name: Appeal to wealth
description: Supporting a conclusion because its proponent is wealthy (or dismissing it because they're poor).

name: Argumentum ad baculum
description: Backing an argument with a threat of force rather than a reason.

name: Argumentum ad populum
description: Claiming something must be true or good just because a lot of people believe it.

name: Association fallacy
description: Judging something by who or what it's associated with, guilt (or honor) by association.

name: Logic chopping fallacy
description: Nitpicking a trivial detail of an argument while ignoring its actual main point.

name: Ipse dixit
description: Presenting a bare, unsupported assertion as if it were self-evidently true.

name: Chronological snobbery
description: Dismissing an old idea as wrong just because it's old.

name: Fallacy of relative privation
description: Dismissing a complaint because 'worse problems' exist elsewhere.

name: Genetic fallacy
description: Judging a claim by where it came from rather than by its actual merits.

name: I'm entitled to my opinion
description: Shutting down criticism by declaring you have a right to your opinion, dodging the actual argument.

name: Naturalistic fallacy
description: Concluding what 'ought' to be the case purely from facts about what 'is' the case.

name: Straw man
description: Misrepresenting an opponent's argument as something weaker, then knocking that down instead.

name: Texas sharpshooter fallacy
description: Spotting a pattern in data after the fact and claiming it as evidence for a cause.

name: Tu quoque
description: Dismissing a claim because the person making it doesn't practice what they preach (whataboutism).

name: Two wrongs make a right
description: Justifying a wrong action because someone else did something wrong too.

name: Vacuous truth
description: Making a claim that's technically true only because it's actually about an empty, nonexistent set.
